# A lakehouse table inside Postgres

The previous chapter moved rows out of Postgres into a columnar database. [pg_ducklake](https://github.com/relytcloud/pg_ducklake)
takes the opposite route and brings the columnar table in. `CREATE TABLE ... USING ducklake` makes
a table in the [DuckLake](https://ducklake.select) format: its rows are written as Parquet files,
its catalog (which files make up the table, their statistics, every snapshot) is ordinary tables
in the `ducklake` schema of the same database, and DuckDB, running inside the Postgres backend,
executes the queries that touch it.

```sql
CREATE TABLE events_lake USING ducklake AS SELECT * FROM events;
```

One database can then hold row tables for the application and column tables for analytics, and a
single query can join them. The lab runs it as the `ducklake` server on port 5443, from the
upstream image `pgducklake/pgducklake:18-v1.0.2` (Postgres 18.4, extension preloaded), and the
notebook measures it on five million events.

## The trade, measured

The same table twice: `events_heap`, an ordinary heap with a primary key, and `events_lake`, a
copy made with `USING ducklake`.

| | heap | DuckLake |
|---|---|---|
| on disk | 301 MB, plus a 107 MB primary key | 78 MB, one Parquet file |
| sum of amount by device | 159 ms | 33 ms |
| daily distinct users | 1,618 ms | 774 ms |
| top ten users by spend | 453 ms | 52 ms |
| one row by id | 0.12 ms | 13 ms |

The three analytical queries read a few columns of every row, which is what Parquet is laid out
for: DuckDB reads only those columns, compressed, in vectors of 2,048 values, and comes out 2 to 9
times faster than the heap even though Postgres runs the heap scans with two parallel workers. The last row is the other
side of the trade. A lake table has no index, so fetching one row means pruning files and row
groups by their min/max statistics and scanning what is left, where the heap descends a B-tree.
Keep the rows the application reads one at a time in heap tables.

## Writes on immutable files

Parquet files are never changed in place, so DuckLake has two ways around tiny files. An insert
below a row limit is **inlined**: the rows go into a Postgres table in the catalog, queries read
them alongside the Parquet, and a flush (or the extension's background worker) writes them out
later. An update or delete writes a **delete file** naming the row positions that no longer count.
In the notebook, updating 1,000 rows and deleting 1,663 left the 78 MB data file untouched and
added a 14 kB delete file and a 19 kB file with the updated rows.

## Snapshots, time travel and a change feed

Every commit is a snapshot in the catalog, with a note of what it changed, and any snapshot that has
not been expired can be read back:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM ducklake.time_travel('events_lake'::regclass, 5) t;
SELECT * FROM ducklake.table_changes('events_lake'::regclass, 8, 9);
```

After the update and delete, the table had 4,998,337 rows and its snapshot from before them still
had 5,000,001. `table_changes` returns what was inserted, updated and deleted between two
snapshots, which is the input an incremental job downstream needs.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A rough edge in 1.0.2

`table_changes` over a range that contains a delete fails with `function struct_pack(...) does not
exist`, and afterwards that connection's DuckDB has lost its catalog (even `DROP TABLE` fails)
until it reconnects. Ranges of inserts work, so the notebook stays on those.
:::

## Partitions, and when they help

`CALL ducklake.set_partition('events_part'::regclass, 'device')` makes later writes split their
files by device, and a filter on device then skips whole files. On a local disk at this size it
bought nothing: 28 ms for the partitioned table against 30 ms for the single file, because reading
one compressed column of 78 MB is already cheap and the row-group statistics inside the file do
part of a partition's job. Partitions pay off on object storage, where a skipped file is a skipped
download (`ducklake.default_table_path` points the files at S3, GCS, R2 or Azure).

## Joining rows and columns

A lake table joins any Postgres table in plain SQL. DuckDB plans the whole statement and reads the
heap side through its own Postgres scan (the plan, condensed):

```text
HASH_JOIN  user_id = user_id
├── DUCKLAKE_SCAN            Table: events_lake   Projections: user_id
└── PGDUCKDB_POSTGRES_SCAN   Table: users         Projections: user_id, pro
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## DuckLake or Doris

pg_ducklake keeps one database and one transaction boundary: the analytical table is written by
the same SQL as everything else and needs no pipeline. Doris is a second system, but it scales out
on its own hardware and keeps analytical load off the primary. A Postgres server running DuckDB
queries is still one server, so heavy analytics there compete with the application for CPU and
memory.
:::
